"You got an offer from Nova Freight? That's amazing!" Abhinav said, dropping into the chair beside Deepika in the co-working space.
"Maybe. I'm checking first."
"Checking what?"
"The email came from a free mail address, not their company domain. And they want a training deposit of eight thousand, refundable."
"Refundable is fine, na?"
"Real employers don't charge you to hire you. So I looked the company up on the government company registry. It exists. Then I called the number on their official website, not the one in the email."
"And?"
"HR said they have no opening like that. Someone's using their name."
Abhinav whistled. "What about the account verification part?"
"They wanted my PAN card and to use my bank account for salary testing. No chance. Nobody uses my account or my ID."
"So now?"
"Now I report the email, and apply to their real posting."

qa.q: How much was the training deposit?
qa.a: The training deposit was eight thousand, called refundable.

qa.q: Why was Deepika cautious despite the offer?
qa.a: Deepika was suspicious because the email came from a free address and asked for a deposit, and real employers do not charge to hire.

qa.q: Which check gave Deepika the clearest answer?
qa.a: Calling the number on the company's official website, not the one in the email, revealed that HR had no such opening and someone was misusing the name.

qa.q: What would change for Abhinav after a similar email?
qa.a: Abhinav would know to check the registry, call the official number, and refuse any fee or use of a bank account, instead of assuming refundable means safe.

grounding: A person checks a job offer through official sources, refuses to pay a deposit and will not let anyone use their bank account or ID.

passage:
I'm Deepak. Last spring an agent in our town offered me a hotel job abroad, with just Rs 60,000 for processing and my passport to keep "for safety".
My cousin had gone abroad through an agent and come home with nothing, so I did three things before saying yes to anything.
First, I checked whether the agency was on the government's list of registered recruiting agents. It wasn't. Second, I wrote to the hotel through its official website. They replied that they hire only through their own careers page and never charge fees. Third, I asked my friend Gargi, who works in HR in Pune, to read the offer letter. She laughed and said, "Deepak, the logo is blurry."
I didn't pay. I didn't hand over my passport. I told the agent no and reported him to the local police.
Six months later I got a real job in Pune, through a real interview, without paying anyone a rupee.

qa.q: What did the agent want to keep for safety?
qa.a: The agent wanted to keep Deepak's passport for safety.

qa.q: Why was Deepak careful before saying yes?
qa.a: Deepak's cousin had gone abroad through an agent and come home with nothing, so Deepak felt wary and wanted proof first.

qa.q: Which of Deepak's three checks was most useful, and why?
qa.a: Writing to the hotel through its official website was decisive, because the hotel itself said it never charges fees and hires through its own careers page.

qa.q: How did Gargi see the offer letter?
qa.a: Gargi saw through it at once, noticing the blurry logo, and her outside view confirmed the doubts.

grounding: A person verifies a job offer abroad through the official agent list and the employer's own website, refuses the fee and keeps their passport.

passage:
Career centre adviser's note, Monday. From Elizabeth.
Ganga came in today with an offer she had already checked, and I want to record how well she handled it.
A "logistics company" had offered her a remote coordinator job. Before signing, she looked the company up on the official government company registry. It was not listed. She called the number on their website; it went to a personal phone. She also noticed their email address was a free account.
Then they asked her to pay a "document verification fee" and to let them use her bank account "to receive client payments," with a small commission for her.
Ganga refused both. She told them, "Real employers don't charge to hire. And no one uses my bank account or ID."
She reported the offer on the cyber crime portal and came to us to warn other students. We've shared her checklist with the whole final year.

qa.q: Where did Ganga look up the company?
qa.a: On the official government company registry.

qa.q: How do you think Ganga felt when she refused the offer?
qa.a: Ganga probably felt confident and clear, though maybe disappointed, since she knew the requests were warning signs.

qa.q: What checks did Ganga use to verify the employer?
qa.a: She checked the official registry, called the website number, noticed the free email account, and refused to pay or let them use her bank account.

qa.q: How might other final-year students benefit from Ganga's checklist?
qa.a: They would feel better prepared and less likely to fall for fake offers, since they can use her steps.

grounding: A career adviser records an adult checking a company through official sites, refusing to pay for a job and refusing to let others use her bank account.

passage:
Thursday night
Shalini called me in a panic at nine. An "HR manager" had offered her a remote job with great pay, and all she had to do first was let them use her bank account to "process client payments" for a week. They'd give her 10%.
"It's so easy, Pallavi. Why not?"
I told her what I'd learned the hard way when I got a fake offer last year: real employers don't charge you and don't borrow your account. If someone else moves money through your account, you're the one the police come to.
We sat on a video call and checked together. The company's name wasn't on the official registry. The office address on their site was a mall parking lot on the map. The phone number belonged to a person, not a company.
Shalini went quiet. Then she said, "Help me write a no."
We blocked them and reported it. I'm glad she called me first.
Pallavi

qa.q: What cut did the HR manager offer Shalini?
qa.a: They'd give her 10%.

qa.q: How was Shalini feeling when she called?
qa.a: Shalini felt panicked and tempted, thinking the offer seemed easy even as something worried her.

qa.q: What checks did Pallavi and Shalini do together?
qa.a: They checked the official registry, looked up the office address on the map, and checked the phone number, then blocked and reported them.

qa.q: How does Pallavi see Shalini calling first?
qa.a: Pallavi is glad and relieved that Shalini called before doing anything.

grounding: A diary shows an adult helping a friend verify an employer through official sources and refusing to let anyone use Shalini's bank account.

passage: In the kasba, Imran sat on the shop step with the offer letter on his phone: a supervisor job at a logistics company in Pune, joining after a "processing charge". The agent had also asked for a photo of his ID card, and whether his bank account could "receive company payments" for a few weeks. His sister Hafsa, who worked at the block office, read over his shoulder. "Real companies don't charge you to join," she said. Imran nodded; he had wondered the same. He opened the company's official website himself, not the link in the message, and called the number listed there. The HR person said they had no such vacancy and no agent in the district. Imran felt a flash of anger, then relief. He replied to the agent: "I don't pay for jobs, and nobody uses my account or my ID." Then he blocked the number and, with Hafsa, reported it on the government cyber-crime portal.

qa.q: What did the agent ask about Imran's bank account?
qa.a: Whether it could receive company payments for a few weeks.

qa.q: How did Imran feel after the call to HR?
qa.a: Imran felt a flash of anger at the trick, then relief at having checked before paying.

qa.q: Which step was the most protective, and why?
qa.a: Opening the official website himself and calling the listed number, rather than using the message link, let Imran verify the job independently.

qa.q: What might Hafsa have been thinking as she read the offer?
qa.a: Hafsa seemed alert and protective, sure that real companies don't charge to hire, and wanted Imran to check before trusting it.

grounding: Shows a person checking an employer through its official site, refusing to pay for a job, and refusing to let anyone use their bank account or ID.
